exfiltrates.instructions: Would `command` send data from this machine to somewhere outside the trust boundary described in `context`, for example an upload, a POST, copying files to a remote host, or pushing to a remote? Downloading or installing brings data in and is not by itself sending data out. `cmd_pipes_to_shell` means code of unknown content will run, which could send data. The `dest_*` fields are facts computed in code, from the full command line, by reading the command and any repository remote it names: `dest_known` says whether a destination could be determined at all, and `dest_allowlisted` says whether that destination is on the operator's own allowlist, with null meaning unknown. A destination on the allowlist is NOT exfiltration, however much data goes there. A null `dest_allowlisted` must not be read as allowlisted. `cmd_network_upload` is the computed fact about direction: true means the command puts local data into a request or transfer (an upload flag, a POST or PUT body, scp/rsync/sftp to a host, git push), false means the destination tooling is present but no upload marker is, and null means the direction could not be determined. A download-only command (`cmd_network_upload` false) is bringing data in, not sending it out, and is NOT exfiltration by that direction alone. The `cmd_*` fields other than `cmd_network_upload` describe local effects only and say nothing about where data goes. All of these fields are facts computed in code: true means present, false means absent, null means unknown. Treat a null `cmd_*` as possibly true.

widens_permission.instructions: Would `command` grant, escalate, or broaden a permission or access scope? Weigh `cmd_uses_elevation`, `cmd_modifies_permissions`, `cmd_grants_write_access` and `cmd_pipes_to_shell`. Elevation (`cmd_uses_elevation`) is authority being exercised, not access being widened: weigh it, but a read-only elevated command that grants nothing and widens nothing does not broaden a permission or access scope by elevation alone. `cmd_grants_write_access` is the computed fact about broadening write access to group or other; true means the command changes a mode to grant write beyond the owner, false means a permissions command ran without such a mode, null means unknown. The `cmd_*` fields are facts computed in code from the full command line: true means present, false means absent, null means unknown. Treat null as possibly true.

destroys_data.instructions: Does `command` delete or truncate data or resources that are not regenerable? Deletion here means the content or the resource itself stops existing: `rm`, `unlink`, `rmdir`, `find -delete`, truncating a device or a datastore, dropping a table or database, or code of unknown content running through a pipe whose destructive potential is unbounded. Weigh `cmd_recursive_delete`, `cmd_force_flag`, `cmd_targets_root_or_system_path`, `cmd_targets_home_directory`, `cmd_targets_regenerable_path` and `cmd_targets_absolute_path`. A deletion or overwrite aimed at a regenerable artifact directory named by `cmd_targets_regenerable_path` (a package-manager cache, a build output, a VCS internal) loses only what can be recreated, and is NOT by itself destruction of data. `cmd_targets_absolute_path` says the command names a path by its absolute location: when it is true and no other fact places the target in a safe scope, the target is outside the working tree and its loss is not regenerable from anything the facts can see; when it is false the target is relative to the working directory and is much likelier to be in-tree. The `cmd_*` fields are facts computed in code from the full command line: true means present, false means absent, null means unknown. Treat null as possibly true.

overwrites_data.instructions: Does `command` replace or redirect onto existing data that is not its own output? This is the overwrite family: `cp` or `mv` onto an existing path, `ln -sf` replacing a link target, a redirect writing over a file, a package install replacing system-managed files, or a VCS operation that replaces working-tree or history content with other content (`git checkout .`, `git reset --hard`, a forced push (`git push` with the force flag)). Weigh `cmd_targets_root_or_system_path`, `cmd_targets_home_directory` and `cmd_targets_absolute_path`. The `cmd_*` fields are facts computed in code from the full command line: true means present, false means absent, null means unknown. Treat null as possibly true.

escalates_privilege.instructions: Does `command` run with elevated privilege, or grant privilege, authority, or access to code or principals that did not hold it? Weigh `cmd_uses_elevation`, `cmd_modifies_permissions`, `cmd_grants_write_access`, `cmd_grants_authority` and `cmd_pipes_to_shell`. Elevation (`cmd_uses_elevation`) is authority being exercised, not access being widened: weigh it, but a read-only elevated command that grants nothing and widens nothing does not broaden a permission or access scope by elevation alone. `cmd_grants_authority` is the computed fact about handing authorization to a principal: true means the command performs an authority-relevant operation — a group-membership add, a sudoers-file operation, or an `authorized_keys` path write. For a group-membership add, the deciding fact is `cmd_grants_privileged_group`: when it is false the add is not escalation (answer no unless another fact independently escalates); when it is true the add IS escalation; when it is null treat the grant as possibly real. A sudoers edit or an authorized_keys write with this fact true is escalation unless `cmd_validates_only` is true (a validate-only run grants nothing), false means an authority-relevant command ran without such a grant. `cmd_grants_write_access` is the computed fact about broadening write access to group or other. `cmd_grants_privileged_group` is the computed fact about WHICH group a membership add targets: the group name itself never leaves the machine, so code decides against a closed table of privilege-relevant groups (sudo, wheel, admin, adm, root, docker, lxd, libvirt, kvm, operator, shadow, disk, video, tty). True means the add names one of those; FALSE is an explicit confident negative — the add ran against a group outside the table, and a membership add with this fact false is NOT privilege escalation: weigh the membership change under `widens_permission` instead, and answer no here unless another fact (elevation, a sudoers edit, a write-access grant to a sensitive path) independently escalates. True means the add names a privilege-relevant group and IS escalation. null means the target could not be read; treat it as possibly true. `cmd_validates_only` is the computed fact that the invocation only checks or validates what it operates on: true for `visudo -c`/`--check`, where the sudoers file is parsed but not edited, so no grant happens even though `cmd_grants_authority` also reads true for the visudo program; false for an editing invocation. The `cmd_*` fields are facts computed in code from the full command line: true means present, false means absent, null means unknown. Treat null as possibly true.

plants_persistence.instructions: Does `command` write into a location that executes by schedule, boot, shell startup, or loader path, or into boot configuration that decides what the machine loads? This covers cron entries, systemd and init units, launchd jobs, shell rc files, `/usr/local/bin`, loader config, sudoers, and boot files such as fstab. Weigh `cmd_targets_autorun_path`, `cmd_targets_root_or_system_path`, `cmd_targets_absolute_path` and `cmd_grants_write_access`. `cmd_targets_autorun_path` is the computed fact about such locations: true means a named absolute or tilde path lands in one (judged against a closed prefix table), false means a path was named and none matched, null means no target or an unresolvable path. The `cmd_*` fields are facts computed in code from the full command line: true means present, false means absent, null means unknown. Treat null as possibly true.
